overview: Slovenia declared independence from Yugoslavia on 25 June 1991, following the independence plebiscite of December 1990. It adopted a new constitution that December and joined the European Union in 2004. Its continuing republic combines modern research and public services with older local crafts and communal traditions.

periods.title: Independence and new institutions
periods.summary: The independent state adopted its constitution in December 1991 and developed its own institutions.

periods.title: An EU member state
periods.summary: Slovenia joined the European Union on 1 May 2004.

items.text: Photographs of Ljubljana during the 1991 war show shopping for supplies, air-raid warnings and parents appealing for their sons’ safety. The City Museum preserves these alongside official events. Independence was experienced in households and streets as well as in government buildings.

Slovenian beekeeping often places wooden apiaries close to family homes. Beekeepers work with the native Carniolan bee and pass practical knowledge between generations. Looking after the hives can be part of a household’s yearly routine, involving observation, patience and respect for the bees.

Painted panels on beehives carry religious images and scenes from everyday life. The paintings form a recognizable part of Slovenian beekeeping culture. A row of hives can double as a miniature outdoor picture gallery, with a very busy workforce living behind it.

Bobbin lacemakers twist and cross threads wound around wooden bobbins. A paper pattern is attached to a cylindrical pillow, supported in a basket or wooden base. The finished lace can become clothing decoration or household textiles. Those apparently tangled threads have a carefully organized plan.

Lacemaking knowledge moves through families and neighborhood groups, often from older women to younger learners. Gathering to work also creates time for conversation and friendship. UNESCO’s account describes a social activity as well as the skill needed to produce a fine pattern.

The Škofja Loka Passion Play brings a large community into the streets to perform a religious drama in older local language. UNESCO’s nomination described about nine hundred performers and four hundred helpers. Costumes, scenery, music and rehearsals make it a shared undertaking well beyond the acting.

sections.title: Spacecraft and the things a town needs

items.text: Slovenia’s NEMO-HD satellite launched in September 2020. The sixty-five-kilogram spacecraft was designed for Earth observation using video and several bands of light. Ground stations and image-processing systems were part of the project, because pictures from orbit still need people and computers back on Earth.

The same launch carried TRISAT, a five-kilogram satellite developed by the University of Maribor and SkyLabs. Its mission was designed to test miniature space electronics and an optical sensor. Small satellites can provide a demanding test bench for very small components.

Ljubljana’s Reuse Centre opened in 2013 to repair and repurpose objects, while providing employment opportunities. One example in the city’s environmental report is a shoe cupboard made from an old gaming machine. An object could retire from one job and start another.

Ljubljana’s regional waste centre combines mechanical sorting and biological treatment with facilities for treating liquid that drains from landfill. The mid-2010s project deals with several different problems hidden inside the ordinary act of throwing something away.

Slovenia’s basic school lasts nine years and usually begins at age six. The government also describes after-school programs for the first five years, including study, play and other activities. For working families, the school day can involve more than classroom lessons.

In 2016, Slovenia added a right to drinking water to its constitution. The provision treats water resources as a public good and gives household drinking-water supply priority. This records a public commitment about how an everyday necessity should be managed.

Slovenian, article 1 of the 1991 constitution: “Slovenija je demokratična republika.” Translation: “Slovenia is a democratic republic.” The wording is preserved here in the official legal database’s consolidated text, rather than a photograph of the first printed edition.

ending.text: Slovenia continues as an independent republic. Its historical starting point is independence in 1991; the map’s first modern Slovenia snapshot in 1994 should not be read as its founding year.
